01 · The setting

One kingdom, different economic conditions

Created in 1815 after the Napoleonic Wars, the United Kingdom of the Netherlands joined the former Dutch Republic in the north with the former Austrian Netherlands in the south. A single patent system followed in 1817, administered from the capitals, Brussels and The Hague.

The south

Early industrialisation

The southern provinces, which became Belgium after 1830, were undergoing the transformation that made Belgium the world’s second industrial nation. Both new inventions and the introduction of technologies developed abroad mattered to this process.

The north

A different trajectory

The northern provinces, now the Netherlands, industrialised later. They shared the south’s patent law and administration, yet experienced a different pattern of innovation and technical change.

Joel Mokyr (1976) used patent records to illuminate this contrast: north and south shared patent institutions, yet followed different paths of industrialisation.

The contrast poses the paper’s central question: what can a patent system achieve when the same institutions serve regions with different economic conditions? Having a patent law was not enough, on its own, to bring about industrialisation.

02 · The evidence

One law, individual decisions

The 1817 system protected original inventions and the introduction of foreign technologies. Officials could reject an application, reduce its fee, shorten its term, or attach conditions. Their task was to weigh novelty, usefulness, and the applicant’s financial means.

An administrative principle, 1817
“to reconcile general interest with individual interest, that this enjoyment be limited to the shortest possible term”

‘Report to the King’, 17 June 1817, no. 1172, Hartsinck & Blanckenay file, NL-HaNA, 2.04.01, 4040. Translation by Wagenaar and Colvin. The report argues for sufficient reward while limiting the public burden of exclusive rights.

How an application moved through the system

An application could pass through several assessments of its legal requirements, novelty, and usefulness before officials settled its terms and fees. Patents also formed part of a wider system of support, including subsidies and loans.

How an application moved through the system

Scroll across to follow the branches.

Access beyond the elite

The archive includes granted, rejected, and withdrawn applications. Despite high standard fees, applicants came from across social classes. For inventions, medium- and lower-skilled applicants were more likely to receive fee reductions than factory owners, nobility, and landholders.

Invention and introduction

Technically skilled applicants were more closely associated with patents of invention; commercially oriented applicants with importation. Administrators treated the two patent types differently, consistent with encouraging useful technology transfer as well as domestic invention.

The findings suggest that discretion served to screen applications and adjust protection, without evidence of systematic discrimination. The model below turns this administrative logic into a decision you can explore.

03 · The administrator’s desk

Enough to make the project happen?

Now apply that principle to two inventions documented in the research. Choose a case and adjust its patent terms. Can you provide enough encouragement to make the project happen, while limiting the cost of exclusive rights?

How this illustration works

The private return and public cost of protection are straight lines. An applicant accepts a patent when it covers implementation costs and the fee, and is at least as attractive as proceeding without a patent. Equality is sufficient.

Effective protection = duration × (1 − restriction)
Private return = return without a patent + 60 × protection
Public cost = 20 × protection

The invention costs 400 guilders to implement; the imported technology costs 250. Both have an assessed direct benefit of 900. The importation that requires protection also has a transfer benefit of 150. The “arrives anyway” applicant can earn 300 guilders before implementation costs without a patent, so introduction remains viable if protection is withheld. These are illustrative values, not observations from the patent files.

The assessed public outcome includes the benefits of projects that proceed, subtracts monopoly costs and an examination cost of 50 per application, and assigns fee revenue a public value of 0.2 per guilder. We show the difference from a no-patent decision on the same application. Examination costs cancel in that comparison. Private returns and administrative assessments are different concepts; this is not a calculation of realised social welfare.

Would the technology arrive anyway? In the model in the paper, protection has no additional transfer benefit when the technology would arrive without it. Here, that applicant can earn a return without a patent. If the patent offer is less attractive than proceeding independently, the applicant declines it but still introduces the technology, paying no patent fee and imposing no monopoly cost.

The model. The model in the paper connects patent protection, applicants’ incentives, and administrators’ decisions. The straight lines and numerical values here are illustrative. “Find sufficient duration” rounds up to the next half-year and reports when the requested term is too short.

Historical fees. Standard fees were 150, 300, and 600 guilders for 5, 10, and 15 years. Officials could reduce or waive these fees. The exercise uses 50-guilder steps, half-year term steps, and a restriction index for clarity; these do not reconstruct every historical policy choice. The requested term sets the exercise’s fee ceiling and maximum duration, with fee and granted duration then adjusted independently.

04 · Compare the rules

Is individual assessment worth it?

The model in the paper starts from a simple idea: applicants differ in the protection they need. A single package of fees, duration, and conditions can give some more protection than necessary while leaving others unable to proceed. For a technology that would arrive anyway, a patent can add monopoly costs without encouraging any additional transfer.

Individual assessment lets officials tailor protection to those differences. Its advantage depends on reliable information and consistent judgement: investigation and expert advice cost time and money, and mistakes can erode the gains. The question is whether better decisions justify the extra cost of making them.

Compare the two approaches for the same four applicants. Here, individual assessment identifies each project’s needs correctly; the slider tests how much extra administration that advantage can bear.

The same offer for everyone

One rule

Every applicant is offered 10 years of protection, a 200-guilder fee, and the same conditions.

Decisions made case by case

Individual assessment

Fees are waived and protection is limited to the shortest term that gets each dependent project started. The importer who would proceed anyway receives no patent.

How much more does individual assessment cost than applying one rule? A 40% increase means administration costs 1.4 times as much. This is an assumption for the exercise, not a historical estimate.

See the four applications and assumptions
ApplicationOne ruleIndividual assessment

Both approaches use the same four hypothetical applicants and the calculation in section 03. The common offer restricts exclusivity by 20%. Individual assessment removes those restrictions, waives fees, and rounds the minimum sufficient term up to the next half-year. Costs and benefits are expressed as illustrative amounts in guilders.

Standard administration is assumed to cost 50 guilders per application, or 200 guilders for these four applications. The slider adds a percentage of that baseline: 40% adds 80 guilders in total. It represents additional officials’ time, correspondence, and technical advice; losses from inconsistent decisions are not included. The baseline and percentage range are illustrative.

In the model in the paper, the benefit of tailoring must outweigh its additional costs. This example assumes officials know each applicant’s costs and alternatives; real officials had incomplete information. It compares two specified approaches, not the best possible uniform rule with the best possible individual decisions.

05 · Implications for policy today

Judge protection by what it makes possible

The research offers questions for contemporary innovation policy. These are implications drawn from the historical evidence and conceptual framework, not estimates of the effects of changing modern patent law.

Adoption as well as invention

What useful activity needs support?

The UKNL system recognised both invention and the introduction of foreign technologies. For policymakers, the question extends beyond generating new ideas to helping firms adopt and adapt useful knowledge.

Proportional protection

How much is enough?

Protection can encourage a project while imposing costs on others. The aim is to provide a sufficient incentive, taking the fee into account, without granting unnecessary exclusivity. Activity that would occur anyway needs a different justification for support.

Practical access

Who can use the system?

The UKNL system was accessible across social groups despite high standard fees, with fee reductions reflecting applicant characteristics. Policy assessment should examine actual access, costs, and implementation, as well as formal eligibility.

Capacity and accountability

When is tailoring worth its cost?

Individual assessment needs information, expertise, and consistent criteria. The UKNL evidence shows that substantial discretion need not imply systematic discrimination; it does not establish that discretion is always fair or efficient. Transparent procedures and scrutiny of outcomes matter.

More patents are not, by themselves, evidence of better policy. Ask whether the rights granted induce useful activity, who gains access, and what the public gives up in return.
Why the institutional setting matters

The same inherited patent law followed different paths after 1830. Belgium saw growing use and codification, culminating in reform in 1854; in the Netherlands, neglect was followed by abolition in 1869. Legal rules alone cannot explain the performance of an innovation system.

Belgium’s later system should not be equated with the uniform offer in the exercise: it was a different historical arrangement.
